summary.value: The paper proposes training an all-atom protein environment encoder to learn general-purpose embeddings through reconstruction and energy prediction objectives. The model adopts an encoder–decoder architecture based on SE(3)-equivariant graph neural networks, where the encoder captures local atomic environments and the decoder reconstructs global structural properties.

strengths.value:
The paper is well written and clear.
The authors created a pipeline that utilizes both structure and energy to get meaningful encodings both structurally and chemically.
The authors showed the usefulness of their approaches on some important downstream tasks.

weaknesses.value:
1. Previous works have shown that MLFF model embeddings (e.g., MACE, ORB, Egret) also perform with high success on downstream tasks such as chemical shift prediction. Comparing SLAE embeddings to these models would be most appropriate in this paper’s context, as both approaches use similar techniques to address the same problem. The training of SLAE’s encoder is similar to that of these MLFF models, except for the added structure reconstruction and the local-encoder/global-decoder design.  Such a comparison would clarify whether SLAE’s success stems from its new training scheme or from the inclusion of energy prediction, which has been explored before.  

2. The authors emphasize the importance of representing proteins at all-atom resolution but ultimately produce residue-level embeddings.  Previous studies have shown that side-chain placement is highly correlated with backbone atom positions, explaining the success of side-chain packing methods.  Since SLAE’s training phase uses inter-residue (rather than inter-atomic) energy terms, it would be informative to test whether the same pipeline without side chains performs comparably. This would reveal whether the all-atom representation truly adds value, given that the encoder and decoder can likely infer side-chain positions from the backbone.  

3. The authors claim to achieve state-of-the-art results on various downstream tasks, stating that they  
   - “achieve state-of-the-art on diverse downstream tasks with transfer learning,” and  
   - “SLAE achieves state-of-the-art or on-par performance.”  
  However, they do not provide comparisons to true state-of-the-art models on several key downstream tasks, such as chemical shift prediction [1,2] and protein–protein interaction prediction [3].  
   It might also be the case for the other reported tasks, though these are outside my area of expertise. The fact that the comparisons for chemical shift and protein–protein interaction are not against the actual SOTA raises concerns about whether similar issues exist for the other downstream benchmarks as well.

[1] Li, J., Bennett, K. C., Liu, Y., Martin, M. V., & Head-Gordon, T. (2020). UCBShift: Accurate prediction of chemical shifts for aqueous protein structure on “real-world” data.

[2] Bojan, M., Vedula, S., Maddipatla, A., Sellam, N. B., Napoli, F., Schanda, P., & Bronstein, A. M. (2025). Representing Local Protein Environments with Atomistic Foundation Models. 

[3] Pourmirzaei, M., Han, Y., Esmaili, F., Alqarghuli, S., Chen, K., Pourmirzaei, M., & Xu, D. (2025). EXTENDING PROT2TOKEN: Aligning Protein Language Models for Unified and Diverse Protein Prediction Tasks.

comment.value:
> Both approaches use similar techniques to address the same problem… the training of SLAE’s encoder is similar to that of these MLFF models, except for the added structure reconstruction and the local-encoder/global-decoder design. 

We respectfully clarify that SLAE and MLFF models serve fundamentally different purposes. SLAE’s auxiliary inter-residue Rosetta energy proxy head is not intended to regress an accurate potential energy surface; rather, it acts as a lightweight regularizer that shapes the latent space and improves reconstruction fidelity. In contrast, MLFF models such as MACE are explicitly trained to approximate molecular energy and forces, which have a very different emphasis. 

SLAE is designed as a self-supervised structure representation learner. While SLAE employs a graph encoder similar to those used in MLFF models, its defining characteristic is the requirement for the decoder to reconstruct the all-atom 3D structure. This challenging objective requires all information needed to recover side-chain geometry, backbone conformation, and local chemical environments to be funneled through the autoencoder’s bottleneck to achieve effective structure tokenization. As one can imagine, strictly local representation of atomic contacts would face challenges in recovering global long-range features, such as beta sheets. We overcome this problem by introducing analytical energy function terms in the decoder, which in turn allows the model to organize the structural feature embeddings in a rich and unique way that allows accurate 3D structure recovery, leading to the good performance we observed for downstream tasks. 


> clarify whether SLAE’s success stems from its new training scheme or from the inclusion of energy prediction, which has been explored before.

Our new experiments as shown in the table above (revised manuscript Table 9) comparing SLAE to MACE performance on downstream tasks demonstrate that SLAE-based transfer learning outperforms MACE embeddings with identical task heads and training datasets. This indicates that the performance gains arise from SLAE’s architectural design and reconstruction-centered training, rather than the auxiliary energy prediction task alone. These new results highlight SLAE’s flexibility and robustness across tasks.

> …it would be informative to test whether the same pipeline without side chains performs comparably. 

Thank you for the very insightful suggestion. We train two additional ablated models to study whether SLAE can achieve comparable performance when provided only backbone atoms as input with objectives: 1. BB_Seq ablation, where the decoder recovers backbone coordinates and sequence. 2. BB_SC ablation, where the decoder in addition also recovers side chain atom coordinates.
Both settings exhibit substantial degradation in reconstruction quality. Sidechain packing partially mitigates the issue, but the  pretraining performance remains far below original SLAE. 
| Model  | Seq. Acc. (%)↑ | RMSD < 128 (Å)↓ | RMSD < 512 (Å)↓ |
|--------|-----------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| BB_Seq | 77.5            | 5.23            | 7.52            |
| BB_SC  | 83.0            | 4.61            | 5.55            |
| SLAE   | **99.9**            | **1.12**            | **1.92**            |


These results indicate that backbone geometry alone fails to capture essential chemical environment cues needed for high-quality reconstruction during pretraining.

> …do not provide comparisons to true state-of-the-art models on several key downstream tasks, such as chemical shift prediction [1,2] and protein–protein interaction prediction [3]

We understand and take the reviewer’s concerns seriously. We clarify below the considerations taken into our initial evaluation choices.

From literature, we had collected customized models and categorized them as “state-of-the-art” models because generally the specialized models incorporate tailor-made strategies to perform well on their respective benchmarks. We thank the reviewer for pointing out the importance of also testing other reported models, and we have now included the results in the revision. The results agree with our initial assumption that specialized models generally have better performance. But we now remove their label as “state-of-the-art” to avoid confusion.

We have also discovered nuances in the dataset prepared for the models suggested by the reviewer and provided the discussion below to clarify that we have indeed used the most comprehensive data available for our comparisons.

Protein–protein interaction prediction:
Pro2Token [3] uses a heavily filtered version of PPB-Affinity which removes all mutated sequences and discards all complexes with more than two chains (detailed in A3.8 [3]). This results in a significantly reduced dataset with 1215 complexes, compared to 12062 complexes used for prior works with which we compare SLAE performance to. Therefore the performance of Prot2Token is not directly comparable against other methods which are trained on the full dataset. 

Chemical shift prediction:
UCBShift[1] and Reference [2] suggested by the reviewer are trained on RefDB [6] containing 1048 entries , whereas our benchmark uses a larger, re-referenced, and quality-controlled BMRB [7] dataset of 3623 entries for consistency and comprehensive evaluation. *10 out of 647 training data entries of UCBShift are in the validation set of the BMRB benchmark, potentially affecting the fair evaluation of the performance of UCBShift. 

The implementation of Reference [2] is not publicly available, therefore we are unable to conduct a fair, controlled comparison with this method on the same dataset. We follow the reviewer’s suggestion to compare our method’s performance with UCBShift [2] along with ShiftX2 [5], and also included results from using MLFF embeddings as shown in the table above (response to comment 1, revised manuscript **Table 10**). Our updated table shows SLAE performing better than all available baselines evaluated on the same data.

**We would like to thank the reviewer again for their constructive suggestions. All new results have been included in our revised manuscript. We believe these additions substantially strengthen the empirical and conceptual contributions of the work and hope they address the reviewer’s concerns.**

summary.value: The authors propose SLAE, a new architecture for learning protein representations. Minimal, equivariant graph encoders handle local interactions (which only see atom positions and no handcrafted torsion angle features, etc.) whereas a standard transformer operates on the outputs of these encoders to model long-range dependencies. Models are trained with a custom objective that includes a sequence recovery task as well as energy prediction. The authors show that the resulting model performs well across diverse benchmarks and boasts an interpretable latent space.

strengths.value: The paper is clearly written (I appreciate the "design motivation" paragraphs) and well-motivated. The experiments are diverse, and the method performs well throughout. Section 5 is pretty nifty too and further helps motivate design choices.

weaknesses.value:
In no particular order:

1. Why is the model trained exclusively on synthetic structures? Is it possible that the method only achieves such low RMSDs because these predicted structures have consistent biases? I don't see this justified anywhere in the paper, and would love to see some e.g. PDB experiments, if possible.
2. The paper states that the model is trained for 30 epochs across 300k proteins on a single A100. I know that the transformer component is minimal, but this seems a bit ambitious to me. Can the authors share the wall clock time of a full training run?
3. Claims of generalizability to complexes and RNA are unsupported by experiments in the paper.
4. Section 3.4 is confusing me; in section 1, it's stated that "the ground-truth residue identities" are provided as inputs, but these are the targets in section 2. It's unclear to me that leakage isn't occurring here and I'll need some clarification from the authors.

Minor nits:

a. The citation for FAPE is given as (Anishchenko et al., 2024); I think the authors meant to cite (Jumper et al., 2021), to which SmoothLDDT is incorrectly attributed in turn.

comment.value:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their detailed review. We are encouraged that the reviewer appreciates our design choices and results. Please find our responses and clarifications to the reviewer’s questions inline below. 

> Why is the model trained exclusively on synthetic structures? Is it possible that the method only achieves such low RMSDs because these predicted structures have consistent biases? I don't see this justified anywhere in the paper, and would love to see some e.g. PDB experiments, if possible.

The main motivations of training on synthetic structures are to ensure dataset consistency and quality, and encourage learning of local variations in structures from multiple instances of similar backbone structures. This has been shown to be beneficial to model training in previous works[1][2]. 

Following your suggestion, we evaluate our autoencoder on a set of 2000 experimental structures randomly weighted sampled from the clustered PDB RCSB, protocol similar to AlphaFold3 training. On this set of diverse, deduplicated PDB structures our model achieved reconstruction quality of all-atom RMSD = 1.20Å for protein lengths < 120 residues and RMSD = 2.13Å for lengths < 512 residues, with no observable degradation relative to synthetic structure evaluation. This shows that the autoencoder achieves robust reconstruction without bias towards synthetic structures. 


> The paper states that the model is trained for 30 epochs across 300k proteins on a single A100. I know that the transformer component is minimal, but this seems a bit ambitious to me. Can the authors share the wall clock time of a full training run?

 A complete pretraining run on one H100 GPU takes 7–8 hours per epoch, with early stopping typically at ~20 epochs. This results in under 160 GPU-hours total wall-clock time, reflecting the actual end-to-end runtime used to produce our reported model. Training on A100 is slower due to both lower tensor-throughput and memory bandwidth, but remains feasible; the end-to-end training time increases proportionally to around 12 hours per epoch, as expected from the hardware differences.


> Claims of generalizability to complexes and RNA are unsupported by experiments in the paper.

We clarify that we do not claim full support for protein complexes or RNA structure modeling in the current submission.
Our autoencoder is pretrained only on single-chain protein structures, so we do not claim end-to-end reconstruction of multi-chain complexes. However, the encoder itself does not rely on residue or chain indices and can in principle operate on multi-chain atomic graphs without modification. We demonstrate downstream utility on complexes through our affinity prediction results, where SLAE embeddings extracted at protein-protein interfaces already perform well. Extending pretraining to full complex reconstruction is a natural next step, and is enabled by the locality and chain-agnostic design of the encoder.

We do not claim current support for RNA or non-protein ligands. However, since the encoder operates solely on atomic identities and 3D coordinates, the architecture is in principle compatible with RNA and small molecules. Supporting these domains requires additional training data and is part of our planned future work.

[1] Campbell, A., Yim, J., Barzilay, R., Rainforth, T., & Jaakkola, T. (2024). Generative flows on discrete state-spaces: Enabling multimodal flows with applications to protein co-design.

[2] Lu, T., Shuai, R., Kouba, P., Li, Z., Chen, Y., Shirali, A., Kim, J., & Huang, P.-S. (2025). Conditional protein structure generation with Protpardelle-1C.

summary.value: They pretrain an all-atom autoencoder (where the encoder does message passing within spatially local atom environments and the decoder uses a global context transformer + ROPE) to reconstruct structure, sequence, and energy values. Using the pretrained encoder as a backbone, they then train several prediction heads for downstream tasks (fold classification, binding affinity prediction, single-point mutation thermostability prediction, and chemical shift prediction). They also find that linear interpolation in latent space corresponds to interpolation between physcially coherent structures.

strengths.value:
- This is one of the few autoencoders, if not the only one, that recovers all aspects of the input (structure, atom identities, and energy values) and that operates on an all-atom level.
- They ablate several design choices, including the choice of continuous vs discrete latent representations (as well as the type of quantization), the effect of the additional energy term in their reconstruction loss, cutoff radii (though only 6A and 8A were compared), and the use of FAPE.
- They achieve competitive results on downstream prediction tasks.

weaknesses.value:
- I am doubtful that the latent space interpolation property is unique to this architecture. This probably applies to other models as well.
- How good are your representations for downstream generative tasks? You can do two sets of generative tasks here, one with continuous latent representations and the other with a discrete codebook. In both cases you can do something like latent diffusion. In the case of discrete codebook you can also do something like autoregressive/masked language modeling token generation. 
- Asides from the novel objective function, not much else strikes me as being very novel in this approach.

questions.value:
- How important is spatial locality for reconstruction and downstream performance? Your ablation seemed to only compare 8A with 6A cutoffs. Using a wider range of cutoff sizes can probably give you a better sense of the impact of locality on performance.
- How important is the all-atom representation? My guess is you can apply the same architecture, but at the residue-level, to get a sense of whether the all-atom resolution is indeed important for reconstruction + downstream performance.
- Any notes on the efficiency of your encoder architecture and its scalability to longer sequences (in case you need to consider a bigger all-atom neighborhood)?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback. We are motivated by the reviewer’s appreciation of our methods and results. We respond to the reviewer’s comments and questions below. 

> I am doubtful that the latent space interpolation property is unique to this architecture. This probably applies to other models as well.

We empirically show that our model results in a latent representation that 1. interpolate smoothly without applying explicit regularization (eg. KL), suggesting effectiveness of pretraining framework. 2. maintains geometrically valid side-chain transitions along the interpolation path.
The latent space contains sufficiently rich local chemical information for the all-atom decoder to produce subtle, ratiometrically consistent changes throughout the trajectory. 

In response to the reviewer’s comment regarding whether other models exhibit similar behavior, we additionally conduct a new experiment on the hinging conformation change of calmodulin. The choice of calmodulin is to explore whether linear interpolation in each model’s latent space provides smooth paths when few observed states were seen in the PDB. Calmodulin structures in the PDB have been observed in three states, with abundant start and ending states but with an intermediate state found in PDB structure 1DEG.  We compare SLAE’s all-atom interpolation trajectory to that of the backbone-only ESM3 VAE using an identical linear interpolation protocol of 50 steps (**Figure 11** in revised manuscript). Along the interpolation trajectory, ESM3-decoded structures show abrupt, discontinuous changes between three different and discrete conformations, as shown between the blue (step 25, 26), orange  (step 27, 28),  and green (step 29, 30) structures. The orange ESM3 models corresponding to step 27 and 28 also produced unfolded domains, which has not been observed in experimental structures. In the corresponding steps 25 to 30, SLAE generates a coherent and gradual series of intermediates with smooth hinge transition.

> How good are your representations for downstream generative tasks? You can do two sets of generative tasks here, one with continuous latent representations and the other with a discrete codebook. In both cases you can do something like latent diffusion. In the case of discrete codebook you can also do something like autoregressive/masked language modeling token generation.

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and agree that generative modeling with both the continuous latent space and the discrete codebook is an exciting direction. The focus of this work is on all-atom representation learning and demonstrating its effectiveness beyond existing backbone- and sequence-based methods; a systematic study of generative performance is therefore beyond the scope of this submission.
However, as a proof of concept, we now include preliminary generative results. In **Figure 12**, we present self-consistent (all-atom scRMSD < 2.0 Å) all-atom structures (lengths 100–300) sampled from a small autoregressive model trained over the 32k discrete codebook. These results indicate that SLAE’s structure token distribution is amenable to generative paradigms, and our local all-atom embedding scheme holds promise for backbone and sidechain structure co-design with latent diffusion or token-based generative models.

comment.value:
> Asides from the novel objective function, not much else strikes me as being very novel in this approach.

We respectfully clarify that the contributions of SLAE extend beyond the proposed objective and include a new local all-atom graph representation, a new asymmetrical encoder-decoder architectural decomposition to achieve 3D structure recovery objectives, and a new direct structure-based pretraining without sequence data. 

We introduce a residue-centered local atom-graph representation that encodes all atomic neighborhoods. To our knowledge, no prior work has demonstrated that such strictly local atomic graphs are sufficient for high-fidelity all-atom reconstruction of global protein folds and can be compressed into compact, transferable residue tokens. 
We also highlight our architectural design where we adopt a strictly local, equivariant geometric encoder originally developed for efficient processing of large atomistic systems. This departs from existing methods, which rely on message passing or sequence-conditioned attention. Our encoder operates directly on raw 3D geometry and atomic identities within each atom’s local neighborhood. Crucially this strictly local geometric encoder is paired with a global transformer decoder, which forces all information required for accurate side-chain geometry, global backbone conformation, and chemical environment to pass through a compact latent bottleneck. 
With these novel designs, SLAE is, to our knowledge, the first method that extracts generalizable protein representations entirely from local atomic coordinates, without relying on models pretrained on large-scale sequence corpus. This distinguishes our approach from sequence-based models or structure-conditioned PLMs. 

> How important is spatial locality for reconstruction and downstream performance? Your ablation seemed to only compare 8A with 6A cutoffs. Using a wider range of cutoff sizes can probably give you a better sense of the impact of locality on performance.

> Any notes on the efficiency of your encoder architecture and its scalability to longer sequences (in case you need to consider a bigger all-atom neighborhood)?

Computational complexity in sequence length is O(N) because edge-indexed tensor operations are fully parallel over atoms.
In terms of local graph radius r, the encoder scales roughly less than O(r^3), reflecting local atom density. For instance the number of average edges per atom increases from 37 to 206 when increasing from 6Å to 12Å. We suggest 6-8Å being the physically meaning radius considering protein sidechain and backbone atom interactions, confirmed by results on downstream effectiveness benchmarks.

summary.value: SLAE is a physically grounded all-atom protein autoencoder. It first constructs a structure-sequence that encodes each residue as its local all-atom neighborhood consisting of atomic geometries and atom types. The residues are tokenized then passed through a decoder to predict sequence identities, 3D coordinates and energies. The SLAE encoder is evaluated on fold classification, protein-protein binding affinity prediction, variant effect prediction and chemical shift prediction.

strengths.value: This paper introduces a powerful abstraction between protein structure and sequence. It is able to encode all of the atoms present in the protein structure in an organized sequence representation that enables convenient decoding of downstream phenotypes.

weaknesses.value:
The paper lacks important ablations that validate the effectiveness of the all atomic resolution. In particular, it fails to compare against sequence-structure co-embedding works such as SaProt and ESM3. It is critical that SLAE outperforms these structure-sequence models that encode the structural embeddings without the same resolution.

There are other works that reason about the all atomic representations of local structures, such as Distilling Structural Representations into Protein Sequence Models, Ouyang-Zhang et al. The paper does not discuss how SLAE compares against such works.

questions.value:
How does SLAE perform against SaProt and ESM3?

How does the all atom autoencoder architecture compare to that in Distilling Structural Representations into Protein Sequence Models, Ouyang-Zhang et al?

We appreciate the reviewer for their constructive feedback, which significantly helped us improve the clarity and rigor of the paper. We have updated our paper with new experiments and comparisons following their suggestions, and address their concerns and questions below with our results.
> it fails to compare against sequence-structure co-embedding works such as SaProt and ESM3. It is critical that SLAE outperforms these structure-sequence models that encode the structural embeddings without the same resolution.

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point about the value of all-atom resolution. We agree that models such as SaProt and ESM3 encode structural information. However, their learning ultimately remains sequence-anchored and primarily reflect evolutionary priors learned from hundreds of millions of sequences on a masked language modeling objective. Contrarily, SLAE is trained for feature extraction on structure only with a reconstruction objective, without bias introduced by training on large protein sequence databases. Therefore, we note that sequence-structure co-embedding models are both benefitted from or harmed by the evolutionary signal learned[1][2], while SLAE’s objectives are exactly to avoid sequence-induced biases and produce embeddings grounded solely in the spatial and chemical environment. Our motivation was to develop a generalizable model and it necessitates the deliberately difficult tasks of removing higher order correlations from sequences. 

Nonetheless, we extract ESM3, SaProt, and ISM (Ouyang-Zhang et al.) embeddings and train the same predictive head on top of them on the four tasks benchmarked in our work, in comparison to the transfer-learning performance on SLAE. We show in the table below (and in the revised manuscript **lines 325-329, Table 9**) that the SLAE framework performs superior across these tasks, highlighting the effectiveness of SLAE’s all-atom resolution representation without sequence pretraining. This distinction is critical as SLAE demonstrates that informative protein representations can be learned purely from atomistic environments, free of evolutionary bias.

comment.value:
> …Distilling Structural Representations into Protein Sequence Models, Ouyang-Zhang et al [ISM]. The paper does not discuss how SLAE compares against such works… How does the all atom autoencoder architecture compare to that in …Ouyang-Zhang et al?

We appreciate that the reviewer pointed out this important relevant work. We have updated the paper to include the reference and discussion (line 117-120). Beyond the downstream benchmarks already presented, we highlight two fundamental differences between ISM and SLAE: **(i)** Like ESM3 and SaProt, ISM augments a protein language model with local structural features distilled into sequence tokens. It remains fundamentally sequence-anchored and inherits strong evolutionary priors from large-scale sequence pretraining. In contrast,  SLAE is a pure structure representation model that learns directly and exclusively from 3D atomic geometry alone. **(ii)** ISM’s autoencoder architecture performs local reconstruction; while SLAE compresses atomic representation into residue tokens, which the decoder uses for global structure reconstruction. 

Specifically, for each residue, ISM’s autoencoder uses a Graph Transformer to local atom types and relative positions into per atom representations, which a decoder takes to decode out coordinates directly in the local frame, not the full protein. In comparison, SLAE’s SE(3)-equivariant graph encoder compresses all local atomic identities and pairwise distances around each residue into a single residue token. The global transformer decoder attends to all residue tokens across the entire protein simultaneously to reconstruct the complete backbone and side-chain coordinates in a unified global frame. 

**We thank the reviewer’s suggestions again. We believe the comparison with ESM3, SaProt and ISM strengthens the clarity of the paper and highlights the key innovations of SLAE: a purely structure-trained, all-atom representation model; and a bottlenecked architecture explicitly designed for structure tokenization and whole-protein reconstruction, rather than structure-conditioned sequence modeling.**

comment.value:
Dear Area Chair, 

We sincerely thank you for the time and effort dedicated to reviewing our work. We also thank all reviewers for their thoughtful comments and suggestions, which have significantly strengthened the paper and clarified the contributions of our proposed method, SLAE. In response, we conducted seven new experiments and substantially expanded our analyses. Below we summarize the major revisions and how they comprehensively address the reviewers’ concerns:

**1. Ablations on all-atom resolution and locality.**  
Removing side-chain atoms or reducing/increasing the local neighborhood radius (4Å–10Å) consistently degrades reconstruction fidelity and downstream performance, confirming the importance of SLAE’s all-atom, moderately local representation. (Section 3.5, expanded Table 1)

**2. Evaluation on experimental PDB structures.**  
Reconstruction on 2,000 diverse RCSB structures demonstrates that SLAE generalizes well beyond synthetic training data. (Section 3.5)

**3. Comprehensive structure-tokenization benchmark on StructTokenBench.**  
Across 11 new tasks, SLAE substantially outperforms FoldSeek, ESM3, and AminoAseed. Ablated SLAE variants show reduced effectiveness, highlighting the value of the proposed architecture. (Section 3.6, Table 2, Table 8)

**4. Comparison to ESM3, SaProt, ISM, and MACE on downstream tasks.**   
SLAE, trained purely from all-atom coordinates of structures, outperforms models that rely on PLM priors and machine learning force field embeddings. (Section 4, Table 9). We additionally clarified architectural and conceptual distinctions relative to ISM in response to reviewer bsEk. 

**5. Expanded evaluation on chemical shift prediction.**  
SLAE achieves the best performance across all baseline models and machine learning forcefield variants (ShiftX2, UCBShift, and MACE variants). (Section 4, Table 10) 

**6. Latent interpolation comparison with ESM3.**   
A calmodulin case study shows that ESM3’s backbone-only VAE produces discontinuous transitions, whereas SLAE yields smooth, geometrically coherent transitions. (Figure 11)

**7. Preliminary generative modeling experiments.**   
Autoregressive sampling over SLAE’s 32k-token codebook produces self-consistent all-atom structures (lengths 100–300), demonstrating the feasibility of generative modeling using SLAE tokens. (Figure 12)

In addition, we clarified the primary purpose of SLAE (reviewers bsEk, XrQz); explained the rationale behind our benchmark choices, particularly why certain prior methods could not be fairly included due to incompatible datasets or unavailable implementations (reviewer XrQz); and provided further details on the model’s training procedure and behavior (reviewer 994h) to resolve any remaining ambiguities.

These additions strengthen the empirical foundation of SLAE and further validate its core design: a physics-informed, all-atom protein representation model that pairs a local chemical environment encoder with a global structure decoder to learn compact, transferable residue-level tokens. This establishes a new paradigm for protein representation pretraining: one that learns entirely from atomic geometry rather than evolutionary priors; and demonstrates that rich protein representations for broad downstream applications can be learned purely through structure-level supervision.


Sincerely,    
The SLAE Authors

summary.value:
The paper introduces SLAE, a novel strictly local all-atom autoencoder for protein representation learning. While the authors successfully demonstrated the method's superiority over existing structure-sequence models (like ESM3 and SaProt) and even specialized MLFF embeddings (like MACE) across new benchmarks, the consensus leans towards rejection. 
This is primarily due to the fundamental disagreement on the necessity of "all-atom" input versus residue-level approximations, with reviewers remaining unconvinced that the marginal gains justify the complexity, especially given the lack of direct comparisons to true SOTA specialized models in some downstream tasks.

The authors solved the concern regarding comparison with structure-sequence co-embedding works by benchmarking against ESM3, SaProt, and even MACE, showing SLAE's superior transfer learning performance. They also resolved the "synthetic data bias" issue by validating performance on 2,000 experimental PDB structures. 

However, the core skepticism from Reviewer XrQz regarding the true value of all-atom resolution (vs. backbone-only inference) persists, as the ablation studies—while showing improvement—did not decisively prove that the all-atom input is the unique driver of performance compared to simpler, well-tuned backbone-based methods.
